title: Compilation & Toolchain
html:
Turning .cpp files into an executable takes four stages — knowing them explains most “undefined reference” and “multiple definition” errors.

The build pipeline

main.cpp
→
Preprocessor
→
Compiler
→
Assembler
→
Linker
→
./app
1
Preprocess
Handles #include (pastes the header text in), #define macros and #if conditionals. Output: one big translation unit.
2
Compile
Parses and type-checks the translation unit, instantiates templates, optimises, and emits assembly.
3
Assemble
Turns assembly into an object file (main.o) — machine code with unresolved symbol references.
4
Link
Combines object files and libraries, resolving every symbol to exactly one definition. Output: the executable.

Useful compiler flags

FlagMeaning
-std=c++20Pick the language standard (c++17, c++23, …)
-Wall -Wextra -WpedanticTurn on warnings — always use them
-WerrorTreat warnings as errors
-O0 / -O2 / -O3Optimisation level (debug → release)
-gInclude debug info (for gdb/lldb)
-fsanitize=address,undefinedCatch memory errors and UB at run time (ASan/UBSan)
-I dir / -L dir / -lnameHeader search path / library path / link a library
-D NAME=valDefine a macro (like #define)

Headers vs source files

A declaration says a name exists; a definition creates it. Headers hold declarations so every .cpp can use them; exactly one .cpp holds each definition.

Undefined reference

Linker error: something was declared and used but never defined (or the .cpp defining it wasn't linked).

Multiple definition

Linker error: two translation units both define the same non-inline function/variable — e.g. a function body in a header included twice.

One Definition Rule (ODR) — every function or variable may be declared many times but defined exactly once in the program — except inline functions/variables, templates and classes, which may be defined in every TU as long as all definitions are identical.

What's the difference between a compile error and a linker error?

A compile error is found while checking a single translation unit (syntax, types, undeclared names). A linker error happens after every file compiled fine, when symbols are stitched together: a missing definition (undefined reference) or two definitions (multiple definition).

Why do templates usually live entirely in headers?

The compiler generates code for a template only when it sees it used with concrete types, and it needs the full definition at that point. If the definition were in a .cpp, other translation units couldn't instantiate it and you'd get undefined-reference errors.
